overall: Draft rule: the freeze sentence is right but incomplete. It only protects identity if a reader can tell a mutable copy from a frozen one, and 'released' is already used undefined in 8.4 and 8.6(a). Add a one-clause definition and a conditional marking MUST. Release candidates need no rule of their own; the release rule applies to each released candidate. Downgrade rule: 'in either direction' is not deterministic, because the changelog's breaking flag is directional (an upgrade test) and a downgrade over a non-breaking relaxation is a tightening that the flag does not show. Both changes belong in 0.9.0 and are not obligations on adopters beyond the marking of unreleased versions.

draft_rule.minimum_text: Once a version has been released, the content it identifies MUST NOT change; any change is a new version. A version is released when the document, or a copy of it, is made available to readers other than its authors as that version, or when the maintainer tags or otherwise publishes it. A version that is not yet released MUST be marked as unreleased, either by a pre-release identifier in the version (for example 0.9.0-rc.1) or by a statement beside the version that it is a draft of that version.
draft_rule.reason: The invariant is 'a version number a reader holds identifies one content'. With 'released' undefined, a maintainer can say 'it was never released' about content readers already hold and edit it; the definition ties release to availability to others, not to the maintainer's private state, so the claim cannot be made after the fact. The mark protects the reverse failure: a reader or agent taking mutable content for a frozen release, which is the same invariant seen from the reader side (8.3 b gives KADS an immutable reference; a derived document has none unless it is marked). It is MUST, conditional on being unreleased, because SHOULD lets an unmarked draft be indistinguishable from a release, and the cost falls only on authors who edit a declared version in place, who were forbidden to do so under the current sentence, so this relaxes the current rule. Release candidates: no separate rule; each released rc is frozen under the release sentence, and the next candidate is a new version (rc.2). An unreleased rc is a draft and mutable. Note the conflict with CONTRIBUTING, which says pre-release identifiers are not used for KADS: either keep the draft statement as the accepted form for KADS itself, or amend CONTRIBUTING; the clause allows both so KADS stays conformant.

downgrade_rule.minimum_text: A change of the pinned KADS version is at least a minor change to the document. It is breaking when a KADS version after the older pin and up to the newer one identifies a breaking change, or, when the pin moves to the older version, retired or relaxed a requirement (which the older version reinstates), unless the document records that none of those changes applies to the covered corpus.
downgrade_rule.counterexample: Pin moves 2.3.0 to 2.1.0. KADS 2.2.0 (or 0.2.0 before 1.0) relaxed requirement 3.4(b) and is correctly marked non-breaking because retiring or relaxing is not breaking (8.3 c). The corpus drops the field 3.4(b) used to require, since 2.3.0 allowed it. After the downgrade the older KADS again requires the field: the corpus can become nonconformant, so the change is breaking for the document. The changelog has no breaking mark in the range, so 'a breaking change in either direction' yields only minor: the wrong answer. Conversely, 2.2.0 tightened a rule and was marked breaking; returning to 2.1.0 only relaxes, so under the three words the document is flagged breaking although no corpus can fail. The maintainer cannot tell from the changelog and the note alone which of the two applies without reading the clause diffs, because the changelog classifies the forward direction. Reversing a breaking change is therefore not always breaking, and reversing a non-breaking change is sometimes breaking.
downgrade_rule.reason: The invariant is deterministic pin semantics: the same pin move should give the same class for any maintainer reading the same two changelog entries. The direction-neutral wording keeps the escape clause (the note may record that none applies) but the trigger is a forward-directional flag, so it misfires both ways. Making the trigger 'any retirement or relaxation in range for a downgrade' uses information the changelog already carries (8.3 c classifies those changes and the changelog describes every release), and the over-flagging is bounded by the same recorded-none escape. A fully deterministic fallback with less drafting: for a downgrade, any minor or major version in range triggers, unless recorded none applies. The rule must be normative: the literal gap is in 8.4 (c), whose range 'after the old pin and up to the new one' is empty for a downgrade, so guidance cannot override it. If left to guidance, the unprotected invariant is that a document pin move to an older baseline cannot be silently classified minor while reinstating a rule.

strengthening: None for the freeze sentence: it relaxes the current no-reuse sentence. The marking MUST is a new obligation, but only for an author who declares a version of their own and leaves it editable; it is conditional and was previously forbidden outright. The downgrade rule can classify more pin moves as breaking than the current literal 8.4 (c), though arguably 8.4 (b) with the 8.3 (c) test already did; the recorded-none escape is unchanged.
reason_needed: The current 8.4 (b) sentence makes KADS's own release branch (VERSION 0.9.0, no tag) nonconformant if the specification is read as a derived document, and 'released' appears undefined in 8.4 and 8.6(a) as the term the new sentence leans on. Shipping the freeze rule without the definition and marking leaves the identity gap open for an exact reader; the downgrade gap is a latent wrong answer in normative text that gets harder to change after 1.0, so it is cheaper to close now.
